title: Text Two 'Advice to Those Who Travel by Sea' (teacher-written in a nineteenth-century style, pupil PDF)
subject: English Language
source: Seeded from english-language/y11 lessons 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33 (Text Two 'Advice to Those Who Travel by Sea' (teacher-written in a nineteenth-century style, pupil PDF))
intro: To understand a nineteenth-century writer's ideas and perspective and how his language and structure convey it

passage.title: Text Two, 'Advice to Those Who Travel by Sea' (teacher-written in a nineteenth-century style for TGA)
paras: Let no traveller suppose that the sea will consult his convenience. She keeps her own hours, and the steam-packet, for all its iron and its puffing confidence, keeps them too. Patience is the first article of a traveller's luggage, and the last he should ever mislay.

The gentleman who complains loudly of the weather has mistaken a steamer for a drawing-room. Let him rather take a place near the middle of the vessel, where the motion is least; let him eat sparingly, keep the fresh air upon his face, and fix his eye upon the horizon, which is the only steady thing in the world on such a day.

Above all, let him observe his fellow passengers. He will learn more of mankind in one rough crossing than in a whole season of fine dinners: who is brave, who is kind, and who, at the first lurch, forgets every other soul aboard and thinks only of himself.
The sea, in short, is a stern schoolmaster; but those who attend to his lessons come ashore better travellers than they embarked.

questions.q: Q4 style : where does the writer advise the traveller to sit?
questions.a: Near the middle of the vessel.
questions.model: Find 'take a place'. Write the detail only: 'near the middle of the vessel, where the motion is least'.

questions.q: Q5 style : give two things the traveller can learn by observing other passengers.
questions.a: Any two: who is brave; who is kind; who thinks only of himself.

questions.q: Write one comparative sentence about how each writer feels during the journey.
questions.a: Text One's writer is frightened, gripping the rail, whereas Text Two's writer is calm and even amused by complaining travellers.
questions.model: Frame: 'Text One's writer feels..., shown by..., whereas Text Two's writer feels..., shown by...'.

questions.q: Find one similarity in what the journey teaches.
questions.a: Both show that travel changes people: gratitude in Text One, better character in Text Two.

questions.q: Turn this list into one integrated sentence: 'Text One is personal. Text Two is general.'
questions.a: Text One's personal 'I' places us inside one frightened mind, whereas Text Two's general 'the traveller' offers rules for everyone.
questions.model: Add evidence to each half and a 'whereas' hinge: 'Text One's personal "I"..., whereas Text Two's general "the traveller"...'.

questions.q: Write a headline and a strapline (subheading) for the guide.
questions.a: For example: 'Going It Alone: Your Guide to a First Solo Journey' / 'How to stay calm, safe and curious when you travel by yourself'.
questions.model: Headline: short, direct, names the topic. Strapline: one line that states the purpose (advise) and speaks to 'you'.

questions.q: Write an opening sentence that speaks directly to the audience.
questions.a: For example: 'Your first journey alone may feel daunting, but every confident traveller once stood where you are standing.'

questions.q: Adapt Text Two's idea about observing passengers into one sentence of advice for students.
questions.a: For example: 'Watch the people around you: a long journey shows you who is patient and kind, and teaches you to be the same.'
questions.model: Select: 'observe his fellow passengers'. Adapt: modern 'you'. Develop: what you learn and how it changes you.

questions.q: Spot the lifting: 'The sea is a stern schoolmaster so be patient.' Rewrite it.
questions.a: For example: 'Difficult journeys can teach you more than easy ones, if you stay patient.'

questions.q: Write a two-sentence conclusion that leaves the reader confident.
questions.a: For example: 'Your first journey alone will not be perfect, and it does not need to be. Pack patience, watch and learn, and you will arrive a more capable traveller than you set out.'
questions.model: Sentence 1: reassure. Sentence 2: echo the guide's key advice and end on the gain.

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, write two paragraphs: 'How does the writer use language and structure to present his advice?' Starter: 'The writer speaks with the authority of...'
questions.a: Two paragraphs: one on imperatives and register; one on the structure (rules first, then observing people, then the summing-up 'in short').
questions.model: Teacher goes through paragraph 1 (the model above). Then shows how 'The sea, in short,' signals a concluding summary, the structural point for paragraph 2.

questions.q: Extend: explain how the final sentence sums up the writer's perspective.
questions.a: Hardship is a lesson; those who learn it become 'better travellers'.

questions.q: Stretch: how might a modern reader respond to 'the gentleman' and 'his'?
questions.a: The text assumes travellers are men, which reflects its period.

questions.q: Core: complete the comparison grid (four rows), then write an introduction and one integrated paragraph in the portal response box. Starter: 'Both writers...'
questions.a: A completed grid and an integrated paragraph comparing ideas and methods with evidence from both texts.
questions.model: Teacher completes row 1 of the grid and the introduction with the class before pupils continue alone.

questions.q: Extend: add a second integrated paragraph on voice (first person and imperatives).
questions.a: Text One's 'I' draws us into one experience, whereas Text Two's imperatives instruct all travellers.

questions.q: Stretch: explain how the difference in period helps explain their perspectives.
questions.a: A nineteenth-century guide expects stoicism; a modern memoir values honesty about fear.

questions.q: Core (timed, 20 minutes): in the portal response box, answer: 'Compare how the writers of Text One and Text Two present their ideas and perspectives about travelling by sea. Support your answer with detailed reference to both texts.' Starter: 'Both writers...'
questions.a: An integrated comparison of ideas, perspectives and methods with evidence from both texts and a conclusion.
questions.model: Teacher goes through the introduction and the first integrated paragraph from the previous lesson's model before the timer starts.

questions.q: Extend (DIRT): swap with a partner using the checklist; rewrite one paragraph using their feedback (what went well, even better if).
questions.a: A redrafted paragraph with a clearer comparison of methods.

questions.q: Stretch: add a sentence comparing how each text ends.
questions.a: Text One ends in gratitude for arrival; Text Two ends with a lesson for all travellers.

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, plan the article: headline, introduction, one paragraph for each bullet, conclusion. Note one idea from each text you will use. Starter: 'Paragraph 1 will explain...'
questions.a: A plan that covers all three bullets, uses at least one idea from each text and fits a semi-formal website register.
questions.model: Teacher plans paragraph 1 with the class: difficulty = delays and uncertainty (Text One's forty-minute wait; Text Two: the sea 'keeps her own hours').

questions.q: Extend: write your introduction in full.
questions.a: A short introduction that addresses the reader and previews the three areas.

questions.q: Stretch: add one rhetorical question suited to the audience.
questions.a: For example: 'What will you do when the train is cancelled and nobody is there to decide for you?'

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, write paragraphs 1 and 2 of the guide (difficulties and advice), using at least one idea from each text in your own words. Starter: 'Travelling alone for the first time...'
questions.a: Two paragraphs in a semi-formal register that adapt and develop ideas from both texts without lifting.
questions.model: Teacher goes through the advice paragraph above, then pupils write the difficulties paragraph alone.

questions.q: Extend: underline every idea you took from a text. Is each one adapted?
questions.a: Each borrowed idea is reworded and developed.

questions.q: Stretch: add a short anecdote of your own to make the advice vivid.
questions.a: A brief, relevant personal example.

questions.q: Core (timed, 25 minutes): in the portal response box (or on paper, then photographed), write the full guide article: headline, introduction, three developed paragraphs, conclusion. Starter: your own headline.
questions.a: A complete article covering all bullets, using adapted ideas from both texts, in a consistent semi-formal register with accurate writing.
questions.model: Teacher shows the first two lines of a model opening, then starts the timer.

questions.q: Extend: proofread for five minutes using the AO5 checklist (capitals, full stops, commas, spelling, paragraphs).
questions.a: Errors corrected neatly.

questions.q: Stretch: self-assess against the grid and write one target for AO1, AO4 or AO5.
questions.a: A precise target, for example 'adapt ideas instead of quoting them'.

questions.q: The writer's main idea is...
questions.a: B) accept hardship with patience

questions.q: Answer the ponder, linking it to Text Two.
questions.a: For example: patience, because, as Text Two says, the sea keeps its own hours and you cannot hurry it.

questions.q: An answer on only one text in Q7...
questions.a: A) cannot reach the top levels

questions.q: Answer the ponder with one reason from each text.
questions.a: For example: Text Two's writer, because his patience and calm ('fix his eye upon the horizon') would steady me.

questions.q: A 15-mark Q7 answer deserves about...
questions.a: B) 20 minutes

questions.q: Answer the ponder.
questions.a: Integrated paragraphs with a comparative connective and evidence from both texts in each.

questions.q: A website article usually has...
questions.a: A) a headline and subheadings

questions.q: Answer the ponder in one sentence.
questions.a: For example: simple and reassuring for a child, formal and reasoned for a head teacher, lively and informative for newspaper readers.

questions.q: Copying long phrases from the texts is called...
questions.a: A) lifting

questions.q: Section B should take about...
questions.a: B) 45 to 50 minutes
